newsitem.title: PERU: Shots heard at Peru's hostage crisis site.
newsitem.headline: Shots heard at Peru's hostage crisis site.

text.p: Several shots were heard early on Wednesday at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima where Marxist rebels hold 73 VIP hostages, police said.
At least one burst of gunfire was heard coming from the rear of the diplomatic compound at about 1 a.m. EST (0600 GMT), police on guard near the residence said.
"We heard the shots but we don't yet know what caused them," a police officer about a block from the residence told Reuters.
The shots were immediately followed by silence. Police surrounding the residence moved into a state of alert but did not approach the compound, witnesses said.

Police said the detonations sounded like shots from an AKM assault rifle. The roughly 15 jungle-trained Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels are known to possess AKM rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the compound against possible attack.
Citing unamed police sources, local RPP radio said three bursts of gunfire from an AKM assault rifle were heard coming from the rear of the property.
Reuters photographers stationed around the residence said they heard at least one burst of about five rounds from the rear of the residence.

Earlier on Tuesday, police guarding the area had moved to within a few yards (meters) of the front of the property in a series of unexplained manoeuvres, while some police threw rocks into the driveway. The purpose of this was unclear.
There were no police within about 50 yards (46 meters) of the front of the residence immediately before or after the shots, witnesses said.

The MRTA rebels inside the diplomatic mansion have fired what were later described by police as warning shots on several occasions during the 36-day siege. The previous incidents caused alarm but no injuries, authorities said.

On Dec. 17, about 15 heavily armed guerrillas swarmed into the Japanese ambassador's home and captured more than 500 people, including government officials and foreign diplomats, attending a cocktail party.

Remaining hostages include Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, President Alberto Fujimori's brother Pedro, top Peruvian government and security force officials and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
